theme: The locust plague; the Spirit poured out, Pentecost foretold
readingInstruction: Read Joel 1:1-2:32. A plague of locusts becomes a picture of the coming day of the LORD. Joel calls for repentance, and the LORD promises restoration and the outpouring of his Spirit. Read 2:12-14 and 2:28-32 slowly.
settingTheScene: Joel’s date is uncertain. Many place him in the post-exilic period, which fits the focus on the temple, priests, and elders and the lack of a king. He writes after a devastating plague of locusts and a drought. He uses it as a warning and a sign: if a locust swarm is this terrible, think of the day of the LORD. The book is short and its main message is sharp: return to the LORD, and he will restore.
observation: “What the cutting locust left, the swarming locust has eaten” (1:4).
“Put on sackcloth and lament, you priests” (1:13).
“Alas for the day! For the day of the LORD is near” (1:15).
“Yet even now, declares the LORD, return to me with all your heart, with fasting, with weeping, and with mourning” (2:12).
“And rend your hearts and not your garments” (2:13).
“For he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love” (2:13).
“I will restore to you the years that the swarming locust has eaten” (2:25).
interpretation:
The book opens with an ugly scene. Locusts have stripped the land. Grain, wine, and oil are cut off. The priests cannot offer sacrifices because there is nothing to offer. Even the animals groan. Joel tells the people to look at this and to pass it on to their children. It is a living picture of God’s judgment.

Then Joel sees something more. The locusts are a shadow of a greater army, the day of the LORD. “Blow a trumpet in Zion.” Chapter 2 describes an unstoppable army before which the earth quakes and the sun and moon grow dark. “The day of the LORD is great and very awesome; who can endure it?”

And then comes one of the sweetest turns in the Old Testament: “Yet even now.” Even now, with all of this, the door is open. “Return to me with all your heart.” The word for “return” is the main word for repentance. And the repentance is not external: “Rend your hearts and not your garments.” Tearing clothes was the visible sign of grief. God asks for the inside to be torn.

The reason to return is God himself. “He is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love.” This is the same description you met in Nehemiah 9 and Psalm 145. “And he relents over disaster.” The fast, assembly, and prayers that follow are marked by hope: “Who knows whether he will not turn and relent?”

God answers. He is jealous for his land and pities his people. He promises grain, wine, and oil, and then: “I will restore to you the years that the swarming locust has eaten.” The lost years are not just forgotten; they are repaid. And the great promise follows: “I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh.” Sons, daughters, old men, young men, even servants. This is the most important promise of the book, and it is fulfilled at Pentecost.
connection: Acts 2:16-21: Peter quotes Joel 2:28-32 on the day of Pentecost. Romans 10:13: “Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.” Luke 15:20: the father runs to the returning son. 2 Corinthians 7:10: godly grief produces repentance. Psalm 51:17: a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise. Revelation 9:1-11 uses locust imagery for the final judgment.
application:
Where do you need to “return with all your heart”? Confess it to God.

Ask what your religion looks like on the outside only. Pray that God would tear your heart, not just your garment.

Trust God to restore “the years the locust has eaten” in your life: the seasons you feel were wasted.
prayerPrompts: Return to God with all your heart, and tell him what it means.
Thank him that he is gracious, merciful, and slow to anger.
Ask him to pour out his Spirit.
